title: The Summer Nobody in Cornwall Would Lend Boulton and Watt £500
conflicts: When the engines first paid: Smiles (1865) says no engine profits were divided until after 1785 and Watt was clear of the bank debt by 1787; Lord (1923) gives net engine income to end-1782 of £3,724 against £9,878 due, Watt ceasing to draw £330 a year in 1785 and £4,000 credited in 1787, but also quotes Watt in 1782 putting 'clear income' above £3,000 a year; the DNB says Smiles dates Watt's first profit to 1787. The story uses the conservative 1785/1787 markers and attributes the 1782 net figure to Lord. Loan timing: Smiles places the £7,000 Wiss annuity and £14,000 bank advance right after July 1778, Lord puts the Wiss deal at the end of 1778; the story says 'over the following months'. Watt's letters are transcribed slightly differently by Smiles and Lord ('no one'/'none', 'run ashore'/'run on shore'), so those lines are paraphrased. Lord disputes Smiles on whether payment terms were fixed from the start.
notes: Episode narrowed from the slate's 1776 'years of losses' to the documented cash crisis of summer-autumn 1778, which sits inside those years. Sources are two nineteenth/early-twentieth-century books drawn from the Soho manuscripts (Smiles; Lord, hosted on the Hopkin Thomas Project), the 1886 DNB on Wikisource, and Carnegie (1905); no modern source loaded for the verifier (Science Museum Group, Kresen Kernow, Birmingham archives and CORE all returned 403). Bacon quote is the 'challenges' stance for my group.
